chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He (peace be upon him) was asked about the prey of the falcon and the dog when they hunt, kill the prey, and eat from it: Do you eat from their remains or not? So he (peace be upon him) said: As for what the bird has killed, do not eat it unless you slaughter it; and as for what the dog kills, and you have mentioned the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, over it, then eat, even if it has eaten from it.

key_terms.صَيْدِ الْبَازِي: Prey of the falcon/bird of prey

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in ruling between eating prey caught by a falcon versus a dog in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between hunting with birds of prey (which require manual slaughter/dhakāh due to their lack of explicit Quranic mention) and hunting with dogs (explicitly permitted in the Quran provided Allah's name is recited). It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the ritual invocation (tasmiyah) as the key condition for validity, even if the animal consumes part of the prey, reflecting the principle of permissibility unless proven otherwise.
